identification.title: I Will Call Upon the Lord
identification.album: Petra Praise: The Rock Cries Out
identification.notes: Written by Michael O'Shields (words and music); copyright 1981 Sound III, Inc.; CCLI 11263. The recording many churches know is Petra's on Petra Praise: The Rock Cries Out (DaySpring Records, 3 October 1989), the band's first praise album, which Wikipedia describes as mostly traditional praise songs in a rock style. The copyright year is 1981 and the release year 1989. The Petra live version adds stage patter and repeated sections that are concert material, not part of the song; the plain congregational form is the two short parts. Reviewed as the song, not as the concert track.

claims.structuralNotes: Two short interlocking parts. The first, three lines, is the singer's resolve to call on the Lord who is worthy to be praised, with deliverance from enemies as the result. The second, four lines in repeated pairs, is a declaration and a summons: the Lord lives, the Rock is to be blessed, and the God of my salvation is to be exalted. God is named as Lord, Rock and God of salvation. Christ and the Spirit are not named and the only act of God is rescue from enemies. The Petra live version arranges the parts with call and response between sections of the audience, which is concert patter and not part of the song's text.

claims.claim: The Lord is worthy of praise, and the singer resolves to call upon him.
claims.subject: God's worthiness and prayer

claims.claim: Calling upon the Lord results in rescue from enemies.
claims.subject: God as deliverer

claims.claim: The Lord is the Rock, to be blessed.
claims.subject: God as refuge

claims.claim: The God of my salvation is to be exalted.
claims.subject: God as Savior

strengths.title: A close setting of David's song
strengths.explanation: The song sets lines from 2 Samuel 22, David's song of deliverance, which also appears as Psalm 18. Its words come from Scripture rather than approximating it.
strengths.scriptureRationale: David calls on the Lord who is worthy of praise and is saved from his enemies - the first part's source.

strengths.title: The living God, the Rock, the God of salvation
strengths.explanation: The second part makes three statements about God himself: he lives, he is the Rock, he is the God of the singer's salvation. The congregation sings who God is, not how it feels.
strengths.scriptureRationale: The Lord lives, blessed be the Rock, exalted be the God of my salvation - the verse the part sets.

doctrinesAffirmed: God as the God of salvation
God hears and delivers those who call on him
theological.assessment: Nothing to correct. The song is two pieces of Scripture set to short phrases: the singer's resolve to call on the Lord, and a declaration that the Lord lives and is to be blessed and exalted. The deliverance from enemies is David's language, which a congregation can hear as the rescue of those who trust God. It is thin on content: Christ and the Spirit are not named, and the only act of God it states is deliverance.

strengths.title: Short phrases learned in a minute
strengths.explanation: Each part is a few short lines that repeat. Newcomers, children and mixed rooms can sing it from memory after one hearing.

strengths.title: A call to worship or opening song
strengths.explanation: Because it is a resolve to call on God and a summons to bless him, it works at the start of a service, or as a bridge between songs.

communal.vocalRangeNote: No published key was confirmed for this review. The melody is short and repeated, so pitch it where the room sings comfortably.

range.note: No chart was read for this review, so the pitches are not stated.

communal.repetitionAssessment: Repetition is the design: two short parts repeat in pairs. The words are Scripture, so it is not empty; the Petra live version adds an audience game on top.
communal.assessment: Easy to teach and easy to sing. The plain two-part form is congregational; the Petra live arrangement, with its call and response between sides of the room, is closer to a concert routine. Churches using the song would do well to use the plain form and keep the Scripture in focus.

strengths.title: God is named in three ways
strengths.explanation: The song names the Lord, the Rock and the God of salvation, so the object of praise is plain.

clarity.assessment: Clear. The language is David's and is not hard. It names no Christ, so it relies on the rest of the service to say how God saves.

synthesis.summary: Michael O'Shields's 1981 setting of David's song of deliverance from 2 Samuel 22, widely known through Petra's 1989 recording. The singer resolves to call on the Lord, who is worthy of praise, and the Lord is declared living, the Rock and the God of salvation. Nothing in it is wrong. It is brief and heavily repeated, and names neither Christ nor the Spirit.

scriptureReferences.relevance: David calls on the Lord who is worthy of praise and is saved from his enemies.
The Lord lives, the Rock is blessed, the God of salvation exalted.
The parallel text of David's song in the Psalter.
